title: Jegadeesh and Titman’s design
objectives: Describe the formation and holding periods behind momentum.

screens.title: Formation and holding
screens.prose: Jegadeesh and Titman (1993), "Returns to Buying Winners and Selling Losers" (JT), rank shares on their past J months. They then hold the winners and losers for K months. Move J and K and watch the two windows.

derive.caption: J = {{J}} months of formation, K = {{K}} months of holding

screens.question: Ranking happens at the start of month 0. With J = 9 and K = 6, what is the last holding month?

widget.accept: Month 5: the holding months are 0 to 5

hints.text: Set J = 9 and K = 6 and look at where the holding window ends.
Holding starts in month 0, the ranking month.
Six months from month 0 are months 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5.

feedback.correct: Correct. Holding runs over months 0 to 5.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count K months, starting with month 0.

byKey.six: You counted six months on from month 0. Month 0 is the first of the six, so the last is month 5.
byKey.minus: Month −9 is where formation starts. The question asks where holding ends.

explain.text: With K = 6 the holding window covers months 0 to 5, starting in the ranking month. Formation covers months −9 to −1, known at the ranking. One ranking and its K months of holding make one portfolio of the strategy.

screens.title: One cohort
screens.prose: We call the winners and losers ranked at one month a **cohort**. JT's 6/6 strategy has J = 6 and K = 6. Here a cohort is ranked at the start of month 20.

state.caption: J = 6: months 14 to 19 form the ranking

screens.question: Which months does this cohort hold?

options.why: Those are the formation months. Holding starts at the ranking month.
That is seven months. K = 6 months start with month 20.
The cohort is held from the month it is ranked, so month 20 is the first.

hints.text: Holding starts at the rank marker.
The rank marker is at month 20.
Six months from month 20: 20, 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Start at the ranking month and count six.

explain.text: The cohort is ranked at the start of month 20 on months 14 to 19. It is held in months 20 to 25 and then sold. A new cohort is ranked every month, so others are held alongside it.

screens.title: The skip
screens.prose: JT's Panel B leaves one week between the end of formation and the start of holding. On monthly data the smallest gap is a whole month, so monthly replications skip one month. J = 6, skip 1, ranking at the start of month 20.
screens.question: Which months form the ranking window?

options.why: That is the window with no skip. The skip leaves out month 19, the month just before holding.
That window is seven months long. J is still 6; month 19 is left out.
You skipped two months. Skip 1 leaves out only month 19.

hints.text: Which month is left out?
The skipped month is the one just before the ranking.
Leave out month 19, then take the six months before it: 13 to 18.

feedback.correct: Correct. Months 13 to 18, with month 19 skipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out month 19, then count six months back.

explain.text: Month 19 sits between formation and holding and counts for neither. Formation is months 13 to 18, and holding still starts in month 20. The skip is a month left out of the ranking, not a month out of the market.

screens.title: Live cohorts
screens.prose: A new cohort is ranked every month and held K months. So in any month several cohorts are held at once: we say they are **live**. Take J = 6 and K = 3. The first cohort is ranked in month 6.
screens.question: Shade every cohort that is live in each holding month.

hints.text: Start with row 6. Only one cohort exists yet.
A cohort ranked in month 6 is held in months 6, 7 and 8.
Each row holds the cohorts ranked in that month and the two months before, never earlier than month 6.

feedback.correct: Correct. A staircase three cohorts wide.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each cohort is live in its ranking month and the next two.

byKey.no-roll: You kept every cohort forever. Each one leaves after K = 3 months, so a row holds at most three.

explain.text: Each cohort is live for three months, so the shading is a staircase three cells wide. From month 8 on, exactly K = 3 cohorts are live. Before that the sample has not yet formed them.

screens.title: Month 20
screens.prose: Later in the sample, with J = 6 and K = 3, no skip.
screens.question: Tap the cohorts that are live in month 20.

hints.text: How many cohorts are live in a month, J or K?
The newest live cohort is the one ranked in month 20 itself.
K = 3 cohorts: those ranked in months 18, 19 and 20.

feedback.correct: Correct. Three cohorts, ranked in months 18, 19 and 20.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count back K months from month 20, including month 20.

byKey.k-plus-one: You included the cohort ranked in month 17. It was held in 17, 18 and 19, so it has left by month 20.
byKey.used-j: You shaded six cohorts, J of them. The number live is K, the holding period.

explain.text: The cohorts ranked in months 18, 19 and 20 are live in month 20. The one ranked in 17 left after month 19. J sets how far back each ranking looks, not how many cohorts are held.

screens.title: One share's weight
screens.prose: Now K = 6, so six cohorts are live, each with an equal share of the book: 1/6. Inside a cohort every winner has weight +1/50 (50 shares a decile) and every loser −1/50. Share A is a winner in one live cohort only.
screens.question: What is Share A's weight in the whole book?

hints.text: The book is the average of the six cohorts.
Share A has +1/50 in one cohort and 0 in five.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average Share A's weight over the six live cohorts.

byKey.no-k: You took its weight in one cohort. That cohort is only a sixth of the book.
byKey.no-fifty: You took the cohort's share of the book. Inside it, Share A is one of 50 winners.

explain.text: Share A's weight is the average over the six cohorts: (1/50 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 + 0) / 6 = 1/300. Equal weights inside each decile and 1/K across cohorts give every weight. A share that is a winner in all six cohorts has the full 1/50.

screens.title: What changes each month
screens.prose: A colleague says the 6/6 strategy "holds its portfolio six months, then sells everything and buys the new winners". Here are the live cohorts with K = 6.

state.caption: K = 6: the cohorts live from month 30 on

screens.question: Well into the sample, how much of the book changes at the start of a month?

options.text: One cohort of six: the oldest leaves and a new one joins
The whole book, once every six months
options.why: That is the non-overlapping design: rebalance every K months. JT start a new cohort every month.
Only the newest cohort is new. The other five keep their weights.
A new cohort joins every month, so something changes every month.

hints.text: Compare two neighbouring rows of the grid.
Rows 30 and 31 share five cohorts.
Each month one cohort leaves and one joins: a sixth of the book.

feedback.correct: Correct. One sixth of the book rolls over each month.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Compare the cohorts live in two neighbouring months.

byKey.nonoverlap: You described the non-overlapping design: everything turned over every K months. JT start a cohort every month, so the book gives a return every month, about K times as many.

explain.text: Neighbouring months share five of six cohorts, so a sixth of the book changes. The non-overlapping version gives one return per six months, about a sixth as many observations. JT's overlapping design gives a return every month from the same data.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose: In holding month $t$ the live cohorts are those ranked in months $s$ from $\max(J + \text{skip},\ t - K + 1)$ to $t$. Once all $K$ exist, the book's return is their average: $$r_t = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{s=t-K+1}^{t} \mathbf{w}_s^{\top}\mathbf{r}_t$$ where $\mathbf{w}_s$ holds cohort $s$'s weights.
screens.question: With K = 1, how do the overlapping and the non-overlapping designs compare?

options.text: They are the same: one cohort, replaced every month
Overlapping holds twice as many cohorts
options.why: With K = 1 only the cohort ranked this month is live. There is nothing to overlap.
Non-overlapping trades every K months, and K = 1 means every month.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the live cohorts when K = 1.

explain.text: With K = 1 the sum has one term, the cohort ranked in month t. Both designs replace the whole book every month. The designs only differ when K is above 1.

screens.title: Live cohorts in code
screens.prose: Write the rule as a function. A ranking needs $J$ months of returns before the skip. So the first cohort is ranked in month $J + \text{skip}$.
screens.question: Complete `live_cohorts(t, J, K, skip=0)`: the list of months whose cohorts are live in holding month `t`, oldest first.

widget.starter:
def live_cohorts(t, J, K, skip=0):
    # the first month a ranking exists
    first = J + skip
    return list(range(t - K, t))  # fix this line
widget.how: Submit runs 10 hidden tests: the start of the sample, the middle, skip 1 and K = 1. Each list must match exactly.

hints.text: Which is the oldest live cohort, ignoring the start of the sample?
The oldest is t − K + 1, but never before J + skip.
`range(max(first, t - K + 1), t + 1)` runs from the oldest to t itself.

feedback.correct: Correct. The rule holds at the start of the sample and with a skip.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Check the oldest cohort and whether month t itself is included.

explain.text: The newest live cohort is the one ranked in month t, so the range ends at t + 1. The oldest is t − K + 1, unless the sample has not formed it yet. The skip only moves the first ranking month later.

screens.title: Sleeves on a desk
screens.prose: A desk runs a £120m momentum book in JT's design, ranked on 12-1 momentum and held K = 12 months. So it has 12 sleeves, one ranked each month. Each sleeve holds an equal share of the capital for 12 months.

state.caption: Sleeve 12 is this month's new ranking

screens.question: How much capital is re-ranked at the start of each month?

hints.text: Only one sleeve is new each month.
Each sleeve is £120m / 12.

feedback.correct: Correct. One sleeve, £10m, rolls each month.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Only the oldest sleeve is replaced each month.

byKey.whole: You re-ranked the whole book. Only the oldest sleeve is replaced; the other eleven keep their names.

explain.text: Each month the oldest £10m sleeve is sold and a newly ranked one bought. Trading a twelfth of the book each month keeps turnover steady. The whole book is never traded at once, so one bad ranking moves only a twelfth of the capital.

ideas: A J/K strategy ranks on the past J months and holds each cohort for K months.
A cohort starts every month, so K cohorts are live, each with weight 1/K.
JT skip a week between formation and holding; on monthly data we skip a month.

formula.name: The composite return
formula.note: The average over the K live cohorts.

summary.trap: Turning the whole book over every K months: that is the non-overlapping design, with about K times fewer returns.

quiz.prose: A 9/6 strategy, well inside the sample, no skip.
quiz.question: How many cohorts are live in a month?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the cohorts still inside their holding period.

byKey.j: You used J. Formation length decides what each cohort ranks on, not how many are held.

explain.text: A cohort is live for its K = 6 holding months, so six are live at once. J = 9 only sets each ranking's window.

quiz.prose: J = 6, K = 6, no skip, returns from month 0.
quiz.question: In which month are all six cohorts live for the first time?

feedback.correct: Correct. Cohorts 6 to 11 are all live in month 11.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The first cohort is ranked in month 6.

byKey.first: Month 6 has one cohort, the first. Five more are needed.
byKey.twelve: In month 12 the cohort ranked in month 6 has already left.

explain.text: The first ranking needs months 0 to 5, so it happens in month 6. Cohorts 6 to 11 are all live in month 11. So the 6/6 series starts at month J + K − 1 = 11.

quiz.prose: JT's Panel B skips one week between formation and holding.
quiz.question: Why does a replication on monthly data skip a whole month instead?

options.text: Monthly returns cannot leave out one week: a month is the smallest gap

options.why: The skip moves the ranking window. It does not change how often the book trades.
JT's Panel B skips a week. A month is the monthly-data version.

options.text: To add a month of data
options.why: Skipping removes a month from each ranking window. It adds nothing.

feedback.correct: Correct. A month is the finest gap monthly data allow.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about what monthly data can and cannot split.

explain.text: A monthly return covers the whole month, so a week cannot be cut out of it. The nearest monthly version of JT's gap is one month. Level 2 shows what it does to the table.

quiz.prose: J = 12, skip 1, ranking at the start of month 40.
quiz.question: Which months form the ranking window?

options.why: That is the window with no skip. Month 39 is skipped.
You skipped two months. Only month 39 is left out.

feedback.correct: Correct. Twelve months, 27 to 38, with 39 skipped.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Leave out month 39, then take twelve months.

explain.text: Skip 1 leaves out month 39. The twelve months before it are 27 to 38. In the reference formula these are months t − skip − J to t − skip − 1.
